questions.question_text: The partial differential equation formed by eliminating arbitrary constants in $z=ax+by+ab$ is
questions.answer: Differentiation gives $p=a$ and $q=b$; substitution eliminates both constants.
For $z=a(x+y^2)+b$, $p=a$ and $q=2ay=2py$; $a,b$ are arbitrary.
The characteristic equations $dx/1=dy/1=dz/1$ give invariants $x-y$ and $y-z$. Thus $f(x-y,y-z)=0$; the first option is a locally explicit form of the same family.

As printed, the final term is $-6D'^2$, so the operator is not homogeneous in derivative order. None of the listed arbitrary-function families solves it for all choices of its functions. A cubic exponent on the last term would also not make any listed option correct.
Integrating twice with respect to $x$ gives $D^{-2}(x^3y)=x^5y/20$.

The integral vanishes for every integrable odd function, but the converse is false. For example, $f(x)=x^2-a^2/3$ is even and has zero integral on $[-a,a]$. The condition does not determine parity, so none of the options must hold.

questions.question_text: If $x=a$ is a point of continuity of $f(x)$ then the sum of the Fourier series is
questions.answer: Under the usual Fourier convergence conditions the sum is $[f(a^-)+f(a^+)]/2=f(a)$ at a continuity point; both expressions agree.

questions.question_text: The half range sine series for $f(x)$ in $(0,\pi)$ is
questions.answer: The odd extension yields a series of sine terms, with $b_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx$.
Using the usual series $a_0/2+\cdots$ on an interval of length $2$, $a_0=\int_0^2x^2\,dx=8/3$.

questions.question_text: $\sin x$ is a periodic function with period
questions.answer: The fundamental period is $2\pi$; $4\pi$ is also a period, although it is not the fundamental one.

questions.answer: For a stretched string with tension $T$ and mass per unit length $m$, the wave speed squared is $T/m$.

questions.answer: The Fourier transform is linear: the constants factor out of the defining integral.
Substitute $u=ax$ in the Fourier integral to obtain $a^{-1}F(s/a)$.
With the convention $F(s)=\int f(x)e^{-isx}\,dx$, multiplication by $e^{iax}$ changes the kernel to $e^{-i(s-a)x}$.

questions.question_text: The Fourier cosine transform of $e^{-ax}$, $a>0$ is
questions.answer: Using $F_c(s)=\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty f(x)\cos(sx)\,dx$, the integral equals $a/(a^2+s^2)$.
Differentiating $F_s(s)=\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty f(x)\sin(sx)\,dx$ gives $\frac{dF_s}{ds}=F_c[xf(x)]$, when differentiation under the integral is valid.
The unilateral transform is $\sum_{n=0}^\infty5z^{-n}=5z/(z-1)$ for $|z|>1$.
The sequence is $0,1,0,-1,\ldots$, giving $z^{-1}/(1+z^{-2})=z/(z^2+1)$ for $|z|>1$.
Expanding $z/(z-a)=1/(1-az^{-1})=\sum_{n\ge0}a^nz^{-n}$ identifies the sequence.
The denominator vanishes at $1$ and $2$, where the numerator is nonzero.

For the bilateral Z-transform, reindexing $j=-k$ yields $\sum_k f(-k)z^{-k}=\sum_j f(j)z^j=F(1/z)$, with the corresponding inverted region of convergence. This identity does not follow for a unilateral transform alone.
Take $p=a\ne0$, so $q=1/a$. Integrating yields the two-parameter complete integral $z=ax+y/a+b$.

Lagrange's equations are $dx/\tan x=dy/\tan y=dz/\tan z$. Integration gives two independent invariants $\sin x/\sin z$ and $\sin y/\sin z$. Hence $\Phi(\sin x/\sin z,\sin y/\sin z)=0$ locally, with arbitrary $\Phi$.

The auxiliary polynomial $m^3-5m^2+6=(m+1)(m-(3+\sqrt3))(m-(3-\sqrt3))$. Thus the complementary function is $\phi_1(y-x)+\phi_2(y+(3+\sqrt3)x)+\phi_3(y+(3-\sqrt3)x)$. Since $F(4,1)=64-80+6=-10$, the particular integral is $-e^{4x+y}/10$. Their sum is the required solution.

questions.question_text: Find the Fourier series for $f(x)=x^2$ in $-\pi\le x\le\pi$ and hence deduce that (i) $\frac1{1^2}+\frac1{2^2}+\frac1{3^2}+\cdots=\frac{\pi^2}{6}$; (ii) $\frac1{1^2}-\frac1{2^2}+\frac1{3^2}-\cdots=\frac{\pi^2}{12}$; (iii) $\frac1{1^2}+\frac1{3^2}+\frac1{5^2}+\cdots=\frac{\pi^2}{8}$.
questions.answer: Evenness gives $b_n=0$, $a_0=2\pi^2/3$, and integration by parts gives $a_n=4(-1)^n/n^2$. Thus $x^2=\pi^2/3+4\sum_{n=1}^\infty(-1)^n\cos(nx)/n^2$. At $x=\pi$, $\sum1/n^2=\pi^2/6$; at $x=0$, $\sum(-1)^{n+1}/n^2=\pi^2/12$. Subtracting the even-index sum $(1/4)(\pi^2/6)$ from the total gives $\sum_{n\text{ odd}}1/n^2=\pi^2/8$.

questions.question_text: Compute the first two harmonics of the Fourier series for $f(x)$ from the following: $x: 0,\pi/3,2\pi/3,\pi,4\pi/3,5\pi/3,2\pi$; $f(x): 10,12,15,20,17,11,10$.
questions.answer: Use the six distinct equally spaced samples, omitting the repeated endpoint. With $a_n=\frac{2}{6}\sum_{j=0}^{5}f_j\cos(nj\pi/3)$ and $b_n=\frac{2}{6}\sum_{j=0}^{5}f_j\sin(nj\pi/3)$, $a_0=85/3$, $a_1=-29/6$, $b_1=-\sqrt3/6$, $a_2=5/6$, $b_2=\sqrt3/2$. Hence the two-harmonic approximation is $85/6-(29/6)\cos x-(\sqrt3/6)\sin x+(5/6)\cos2x+(\sqrt3/2)\sin2x$.

questions.question_text: A string is stretched and fastened to two points $l$ apart. Motion is started by displacing the string into the form $50(lx-x^2)$ from which it is released at time $t=0$. Find the displacement at any point on the string at a distance $x$ from one end at time $t$.
questions.answer: Take $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$, fixed ends and $u_t(x,0)=0$. Separation gives $u=\sum_{n\ge1}B_n\sin(n\pi x/l)\cos(n\pi ct/l)$, where $B_n=\frac2l\int_0^l50(lx-x^2)\sin(n\pi x/l)\,dx=\frac{200l^2[1-(-1)^n]}{n^3\pi^3}$. Therefore $u=\frac{400l^2}{\pi^3}\sum_{n\ge1,\ n\text{ odd}}\frac{\sin(n\pi x/l)\cos(n\pi ct/l)}{n^3}$.

questions.question_text: The ends A and B of a rod 30 cm long have their temperature kept at $20^\circ\mathrm C$ and $80^\circ\mathrm C$ until steady state prevails. The temperature at the end B is then suddenly reduced to $60^\circ\mathrm C$ and that of A is raised to $40^\circ\mathrm C$ and maintained the same. Find the temperature distribution.
questions.answer: Let $x$ be in cm from A and $u_t=\alpha^2u_{xx}$. The initial steady profile is $20+2x$ and the new steady profile is $40+2x/3$. Their difference is $-20+4x/3$, whose sine coefficients on $(0,30)$ are $B_n=-40[1+(-1)^n]/(n\pi)$. Thus $u(x,t)=40+2x/3-\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{40[1+(-1)^n]}{n\pi}\sin(n\pi x/30)e^{-\alpha^2n^2\pi^2t/900}$. The initial and new boundary values are incompatible exactly at the endpoints at $t=0$.

questions.question_text: Find the Fourier transform of $f(x)=1$ for $|x|<a$, $f(x)=0$ for $|x|>a>0$, and hence evaluate (i) $\int_0^\infty\frac{\sin t}{t}\,dt$; (ii) $\int_0^\infty(\frac{\sin x}{x})^2\,dx$.
questions.answer: With $\widehat f(s)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)e^{-isx}\,dx$, $\widehat f(s)=2\sin(as)/s$ (value $2a$ at $s=0$). Fourier inversion at $x=0$ gives $1=(2/\pi)\int_0^\infty\sin(as)/s\,ds$, so (i) is $\pi/2$. Parseval gives $2a=(1/2\pi)\int_{-\infty}^\infty4\sin^2(as)/s^2\,ds$, hence (ii) is $\pi/2$ after scaling.

questions.question_text: Find the Fourier cosine transform of $e^{-ax}$, $a>0$. Hence deduce the value of $\int_0^\infty\frac{dx}{(x^2+1)(x^2+4)}$.
questions.answer: For the normalized cosine transform, $F_c(s)=\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-ax}\cos(sx)\,dx=\sqrt{2/\pi}\,a/(a^2+s^2)$. Parseval applied to $e^{-x}$ and $e^{-2x}$ gives $1/3=\frac4\pi\int_0^\infty\frac{ds}{(s^2+1)(s^2+4)}$. Therefore the integral is $\pi/12$.

The first sequence is undefined at $n=0,1$, so its unilateral transform needs a starting-index convention. If those two values are set to zero, put $t=1/z$ and sum from $n=2$: $\sum t^n/[n(n-1)]=t+(1-t)\log(1-t)$. For (ii), partial fractions give $1/(n+1)+2/(n+2)$, so $Z=-\log(1-t)/t+2[-\log(1-t)-t]/t^2$, $t=1/z$, $|z|>1$.

questions.question_text: Solve the difference equation using Z-transform: $y_{n+2}-3y_{n+1}-10y_n=0$, $y_0=1$, $y_1=0$.
questions.answer: Let $Y=\sum_{n\ge0}y_nz^{-n}$. Applying the shift formulas gives $(z^2-3z-10)Y=z^2-3z$, so $Y=z(z-3)/[(z-5)(z+2)]=(2/7)z/(z-5)+(5/7)z/(z+2)$. Inverting gives $y_n=(2/7)5^n+(5/7)(-2)^n$.
